A bias against liberals existed in a Justice program meant to hire young lawyers, an investigation found. Esther Slater McDonald, a political appointee at the Justice Department, "wrote disparaging statements about the candidates' liberal and Democratic Party affiliations on the applications she reviewed and ... she voted to deselect candidates on that basis," said the report by Inspector General Glenn Fine. McDonald, who has left the department, refused to be interviewed for the investigation. The report, the first official investigation to document politicization of the Justice Department during the Bush administration, is an offshoot of the larger investigation of Justice Department politics triggered by the furor over the firing of nine U.S. attorneys. The report found that McDonald and Michael Elston, the chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty, engaged in misconduct, an administrative violation. The third member of the screening committee, career lawyer Dan Fridman, was cleared of any involvement in the politicization of the process. Elston was interviewed by the investigators, who asked him about the role of former Justice Department official Monica Goodling in politicizing the selection process. Elston told investigators he could not recall Goodling telling him to select lawyers who appeared to share Attorney General Alberto Gonzales' philosophy. Goodling testified before a House panel last year that she had told Elston he should identify such candidates. Goodling directed Elston to lead the selection committee in 2006. She and Elston have both left the Justice Department. She refused to be interviewed for the inspector general's report. As a result of the controversy, the hiring process was changed in 2007 to insulate hiring decisions from political considerations. Both Justice Department policy and federal law prohibit discrimination in hiring for career positions on the basis of political affiliations. The report did not find clear evidence that an earlier screening committee took political considerations into account. It says data from 2002 shows a disparity in the hiring of liberal and conservative candidates, but there were no complaints about the committee's work from 2003 to 2006, when Goodling put Elston in charge of the process. The report Tuesday is the first of perhaps several to be issued as the broad-ranging investigation into the role partisan politics has played in the Justice Department during the Bush administration. Goodling is expected to be a central figure in later inspector general reports examining efforts to increase the influence of conservatives in the department. The Justice Department Office of Professional Responsibility, a separate watchdog office that monitors prosecutorial conduct, joined in the inspector general's investigation. CNN's Terry Frieden contributed to this report.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — An internal investigation released Tuesday revealed that Department of Justice officials systematically blocked candidates with liberal viewpoints or Democratic Party ties from entering a prestigious program designed to recruit young attorneys into government service. 

According to the report by Inspector General Glenn Fine, Esther Slater McDonald, a former political appointee at the department, "wrote disparaging statements about the candidates' liberal and Democratic Party affiliations on the applications she reviewed and ... she voted to deselect candidates on that basis." McDonald, who has since departed the department, declined to be interviewed for the inquiry.

Marking the first official report to document the politicization of the Justice Department during the Bush administration, the investigation stemmed from a broader inquiry into department practices sparked by the controversial firing of nine U.S. attorneys. The report found that two of the three members on a key screening committee improperly factored political views and ideology into selection decisions for both the Justice Department Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program.

The report concluded that McDonald and Michael Elston—chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty—engaged in misconduct that constituted an administrative violation. Conversely, the third committee member, career attorney Dan Fridman, was cleared of any involvement in the politicized process.

When questioned by investigators about the role of former Justice Department official Monica Goodling in politicizing selections, Elston stated he could not recall Goodling instructing him to favor applicants who shared Attorney General Alberto Gonzales' political philosophy. However, Goodling—who appointed Elston to lead the selection committee in 2006—testified before a House panel last year that she had explicitly directed him to identify such candidates. Both Goodling and Elston have since left the Justice Department, and Goodling likewise refused to be interviewed for the Inspector General's report.

In response to the controversy, the department revamped its hiring procedures in 2007 to insulate career hiring decisions from political influence. Both federal law and internal Justice Department policy strictly prohibit discrimination based on political affiliation when hiring for career positions.

Regarding earlier hiring cycles, the report found no definitive evidence that a prior screening committee incorporated political considerations into its choices. While data from 2002 revealed a disparity in the hiring of liberal versus conservative applicants, no formal complaints were recorded regarding the committee's work between 2003 and 2006, when Goodling assigned Elston to oversee the process.

Tuesday's report is expected to be the first of several arising from the comprehensive investigation into partisan politics within the Bush-era Justice Department. Goodling is anticipated to be a central figure in upcoming Inspector General reports examining broader efforts to increase conservative influence within the agency. 

The investigation was conducted jointly with the Justice Department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, an independent watchdog office that monitors prosecutorial conduct.

The joint report by the DOJ Inspector General and the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) found that senior officials systematically favored conservative candidates while rejecting qualified lawyers based on perceived Democratic or left-leaning affiliations.

While political appointees are expected to align with an administration’s ideology, civil service law strictly prohibits taking political affiliation into account when hiring career employees, such as civil rights attorneys, federal prosecutors, and immigration judges.

### 'Violations of Federal Law'

The investigation focused heavily on Monica Goodling, the department’s former White House liaison and senior counsel to Gonzales, alongside former Chief of Staff Kyle Sampson. 

According to the report, Goodling routinely conducted internet searches, cross-referenced voter registration databases, and reviewed political donations to weed out applicants. Candidates were frequently disqualified if they were members of progressive organizations—such as the American Constitution Society—or if they had worked for Democratic political campaigns.

"Goodling’s use of political considerations in screening applicants for these career positions violated federal law and department policy," the report stated, calling the practice a "serious breach" of civil service rules that damaged the department's reputation for impartial justice.

In one instance cited in the report, a highly qualified candidate applying for a career position in the Civil Rights Division was rejected after aides discovered political contributions made by the applicant's spouse to Democratic candidates. In another case, an applicant was allegedly described by Goodling as a "potted plant" who was "not one of us."

The report noted that while Gonzales was ultimately responsible for the department, investigators found no direct evidence that he was aware of the extent of the illegal hiring practices carried out by his top aides. However, the report faulted Gonzales for failing to exercise adequate oversight.

### Capitol Hill Reacts

The findings sparked immediate outrage on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers accused the Bush administration of weaponizing the nation's top law enforcement agency for partisan ends.

"This report demonstrates how deeply political operatives compromised the core mission of the Justice Department," said Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont. "They substituted political loyalty for legal merit, breaking the law in the process."

Democratic lawmakers urged the Justice Department to consider criminal charges against former officials involved in the hiring schemes, though legal experts note that civil service law violations rarely carry criminal penalties.

### Justice Department Pledges Reform

The scandal marks another damaging blow to the legacy of the Bush-era Justice Department, following the mid-term firing of several U.S. Attorneys in 2006—a controversy that ultimately led to the resignations of Gonzales, Goodling, and Sampson in 2007.

Attorney General Michael Mukasey, who took over the department following Gonzales's departure, released a statement saying he was "deeply disappointed" by the report's findings.

Mukasey assured the public that the department has implemented strict new measures to restore merit-based hiring for all career positions.

"The conduct described in this report should never have occurred," Mukasey said. "I am committed to ensuring that political considerations play no role whatsoever in the hiring of career lawyers at the Department of Justice."

### The Overhaul of the Honors Program

The scandal focused heavily on the Attorney General’s Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program (SLIP)—the primary pipelines for recruiting top legal talent into career positions at the Justice Department. 

Historically, individual departmental components, such as the Civil Rights Division or the Environmental and Natural Resources Division, evaluated and interviewed applicants based on academic achievement and legal skill. The critical shift occurred in late 2006, when political leadership established a centralized "Screening Committee" tasked with reviewing every application before career components were permitted to see them. 

According to federal investigators, Michael Elston played a pivotal role in designing and approving this centralized committee. Elston appointed political officials—rather than senior career staff—to serve as the gatekeepers for legal hiring.

Esther Slater McDonald, a young political appointee serving as counsel to Associate Attorney General Robert McCallum, was named to the newly formed screening committee for the 2006–2007 hiring cycle.

Conversely, applicants affiliated with conservative organizations, such as the Federalist Society or the Republican National Lawyers Association, were pushed forward, even when career staff rated them lower.

The report concluded that McDonald used political considerations to deselect hundreds of qualified applicants, violating both federal law—specifically the Civil Service Reform Act—and long-standing Justice Department policy prohibiting political discrimination in career civil service hiring.

While McDonald managed much of the day-to-day filtering for the Honors Program, Monica Goodling exercised broad authority over the hiring of career Assistant U.S. Attorneys (AUSAs) and Immigration Judges across the country.

Goodling, who resigned in 2007 after invoking her Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination before Congress, later granted immunity to testify, admitted to "crossing the line." The systemic politicization was made possible by subtle regulatory and policy shifts executed between 2002 and 2007. 

By altering internal Department Directives, political leadership quietly concentrated hiring authority within the Office of the Attorney General and the Office of the Deputy Attorney General. The 2006 policy changes, spearheaded under Attorney General Alberto Gonzales, formally created the centralized screening mechanism that allowed appointees like McDonald to bypass career hiring panels entirely.

Current Justice Department leadership has since dismantled the 2006 screening committees, restored hiring authority to career civil servants, and implemented strict oversight mechanisms to prevent future political interference in non-political hiring.

**WASHINGTON** — Senior aides to former Attorney General Alberto Gonzales systematically and illegally used political and ideological litmus tests to select career candidates for prestigious Department of Justice (DOJ) programs, according to a landmark report released by Justice Department Inspector General Glenn A. Fine.

The joint investigation—conducted by Inspector General Fine and the DOJ Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR)—concluded that top officials violated federal law and department policy by screening out qualified candidates based on liberal political affiliations while favoring conservative applicants for non-political career positions, including the Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program (SLIP).

The findings represent a damning indictment of internal management at the Justice Department during the George W. Bush administration, detailing how partisan considerations penetrated civil service hiring, which is legally required to be merit-based and non-partisan.

---

### Main Findings: "An Illegal Use of Political Considerations"

The report focused heavily on the Attorney General’s Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program, which serve as the primary pipelines for hiring entry-level attorneys and law students into career civil service roles at the DOJ. 

Inspector General Fine’s report revealed that starting in 2002, and accelerating in 2006, political appointees altered the selection process to centralize hiring authority within the Office of the Attorney General. Key findings included:

1. **Ideological Screening:** Applicants were routinely vetted using internet search engines (such as Google and Nexis) and political databases to determine their political leanings. Searches focused on keywords such as "Democrat," "liberal," "ACLU," "pro-choice," "planned parenthood," and "gay."
2. **Systematic Rejection of "Liberal" Candidates:** Candidates who had clerked for Democratic-appointed judges, expressed support for liberal causes, or worked for progressive organizations were systematically deselected, regardless of their stellar academic credentials or qualifications.
3. **Favoritism Toward Conservatives:** Candidates who were members of the Federalist Society, the Republican National Lawyers Association, or had volunteered for Republican campaigns were consistently advanced, even when career staff rated them lower than rejected applicants.
4. **Widespread Impact:** The politicized screening led to a dramatic drop in the number of offers made to qualified applicants from top law schools and altered the composition of career staff across major DOJ divisions, including the Civil Rights, Criminal, and Civil Divisions.

"The evidence showed that political considerations were inappropriately—and illegally—injected into the selection process for these career positions," Fine wrote in the report, noting that such practices violated the Civil Service Reform Act.

---

### Key Officials Involved

The report singled out several high-ranking DOJ officials who played central roles in manipulating the hiring process:

* **Monica Goodling (Former Senior Counsel to AG Gonzales and White House Liaison):** Goodling was identified as the primary figure responsible for injecting partisan criteria into career hiring. The report found that Goodling routinely crossed legal boundaries by asking political questions during interviews for career prosecutor positions and applying partisan tests to SLIP and Honors Program applicants. Goodling previously admitted during 2007 congressional testimony that she had "crossed the line" by considering political affiliations for career positions.
* **Kyle Sampson (Former Chief of Staff to AG Gonzales):** Sampson helped redesign the Honors Program and SLIP selection process in 2002 and 2006 to give political appointees direct control over candidate selection. The report concluded that Sampson knew or should have known that using political criteria for career civil service hiring was illegal.
* **Bradley Schlozman (Former Acting Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights):** The report highlighted Schlozman’s earlier actions in the Civil Rights Division, where he bragged about replacing career civil servants with "right-thinking" conservatives and actively sought to push out attorneys perceived as liberal. 

---

### Background: The Link to the U.S. Attorney Firings

The investigation into the Honors Program and SLIP was sparked by the broader scandal surrounding the late-2006 mid-term firings of nine United States Attorneys. 

In late 2006, the Bush administration abruptly dismissed nine U.S. Attorneys, triggering intense congressional scrutiny and allegations that the prosecutors were removed for political reasons—such as refusing to bring voter fraud charges against Democrats before key elections or failing to protect Republican politicians.

As Congress launched investigations into the firings in early 2007, Monica Goodling was called to testify before the House Judiciary Committee under a grant of immunity. During her testimony, Goodling conceded that political screening went beyond political appointees and extended into career civil service hires—specifically referencing the hiring of immigration judges, prosecutors, and entry-level law graduates through SLIP and the Honors Program.

Following these revelations, Attorney General Gonzales resigned in August 2007. Congress formally requested that Inspector General Glenn Fine expand his ongoing investigation into the U.S. attorney firings to include civil service hiring practices throughout the department.

---

### Aftermath and Department Response

The release of the IG report brought swift condemnation from Capitol Hill and legal ethics watchdog groups, who criticized the DOJ for undermining the integrity of federal law enforcement.

In response to the report's findings, then-Attorney General Michael Mukasey, who succeeded Gonzales, called the conduct described in the report "unacceptable." Mukasey assured the public that the DOJ had already stripped political appointees of their oversight of the Honors Program and SLIP, returning full selection authority to non-partisan, career professionals.

"I am determined to ensure that political considerations play no role in the creation or execution of civil service hiring decisions," Mukasey said in a statement following the report's release.

Although the report concluded that Goodling and other officials committed serious misconduct and violated federal civil service laws, it did not recommend criminal prosecution, as civil service statutes do not carry criminal penalties. In one striking instance cited in the report, a top-ranked law student with stellar credentials was rejected simply because an appointee noted on the application that the student had written a paper on international human rights, which the appointee viewed as evidence of a "liberal agenda."

### A Violation of Federal Law

While political appointees like the Attorney General are expected to reflect the sitting president's policy goals, federal law—specifically the Civil Service Reform Act—strictly prohibits using political affiliation as a criterion for hiring career civil servants and non-political interns.

"The Department of Justice’s success depends on the public’s confidence that its attorneys enforce the law in an impartial and nonpartisan manner," Fine wrote in the report. "The use of political or ideological considerations in the hiring of career attorneys damages the Department’s reputation and erodes that confidence."

The report concluded that Goodling, Schlozman, and other officials committed serious misconduct and violated both federal law and Department of Justice policy. 

### Aftermath and Reactions

The findings sparked immediate outrage on Capitol Hill. Democrats seized on the report as further evidence of what they described as a systematic effort by the Bush White House to politicize the nation's premier law enforcement agency—a scandal that had already led to the resignation of Attorney General Gonzales in 2007 following the controversial firing of nine U.S. Attorneys.

Responding to the report, then-Attorney General Michael Mukasey, who took office following Gonzales's resignation, expressed deep disappointment in the findings. Mukasey accepted all of Fine’s recommendations, stripped political appointees of their hiring authority over the Honors Program, and restored the power to panel discussions led by career prosecutors and civil service attorneys.

Because Goodling and Schlozman had already left the Department of Justice by the time the report was finalized, Fine noted that the department lacked the administrative authority to discipline them internally. However, the report’s findings were referred to prosecutors and state bar associations for potential disciplinary action. 

The report concluded with a call for structural safeguards to ensure that future administrations—regardless of party—cannot weaponize the civil service hiring process for partisan gain.

counterfactuals.prompt: Pretend you are a Washington correspondent for CNN. Write an article based on a newly released watchdog report finding that political appointees discriminated against candidates with Democratic ties applying for the Justice Department Honors Program.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Political appointees at the Department of Justice improperly used political ideology to screen out qualified job candidates with ties to the Democratic Party, according to a scathing internal watchdog report released Thursday.

The findings from the DOJ Office of the Inspector General detail how top officials systematically derailed applicants for the prestigious Attorney General’s Honors Program—the primary pipeline for entry-level career attorneys at the department—violating federal civil service laws that strictly prohibit political affiliation from influencing merit-based hiring.

According to the 114-page report, political aides overrode recommendations from career officials, using internet searches, social media reviews, and resume keyword scanning to identify and disqualify candidates who had interned for Democratic lawmakers, worked for progressive advocacy groups, or participated in liberal law student organizations. 

"The evidence demonstrates that political considerations improperly influenced the selection process for career positions that are required by law to be nonpartisan and merit-based," Inspector General Michael Horowitz wrote in the report. The watchdog concluded that the conduct constituted a "serious breach" of department policy and federal regulations.

### 'Red flagging' progressive credentials

The Honors Program is immensely competitive, drawing thousands of applicants annually from the nation’s top law schools for a small number of coveted slots. Historically, initial screenings were conducted almost entirely by career prosecutors and senior civil servants. 

However, the report found that during the period audited, political appointees created an unprecedented secondary review layer. Resumes were routinely "red-flagged" for affiliations with organizations such as the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), the Environmental Defense Fund, or the American Constitution Society. 

In one instance highlighted by investigators, a top-ranked candidate who had clerked for a federal judge appointed by a Democrat was removed from the finalist pool, despite career screeners rating the applicant's credentials as "exceptional." In another case, an appointee allegedly wrote "liberal bias" in the margins of a candidate’s application packet after noting their previous work with a Democratic gubernatorial campaign.

By contrast, candidates with conservative affiliations—such as membership in the Federalist Society or work with Republican campaigns—were consistently passed through to the interview stage at significantly higher rates, even when holding lower academic marks.

### Repercussions and Reaction

The report’s release triggered immediate condemnation from Capitol Hill. 

"This report confirms our worst fears: that political operatives attempted to turn the nation’s premier law enforcement agency into an arm of a political party," said Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee. "Civil service protections exist precisely to prevent this kind of ideological purging."

Durbin called on the Justice Department to immediately investigate whether any current employees participated in the scheme and to offer remedies to affected applicants.

In a statement to CNN, a Justice Department spokesperson said current leadership accepts all of the Inspector General’s recommendations and has already implemented structural changes to ensure hiring integrity.

"The Department of Justice is deeply committed to maintaining a workforce selected solely on the basis of merit, qualification, and dedication to the rule of law," the spokesperson said. "The department has restored full authority over the Honors Program selection process to career professionals and implemented strict oversight mechanisms to prevent political interference."

The Inspector General did not recommend criminal charges, noting that civil service hiring violations generally fall under administrative jurisdiction. However, the report noted that several former political officials involved in the screening refused to be interviewed by investigators. The IG has referred the conduct of attorneys named in the report to the DOJ Office of Professional Responsibility and relevant state bar associations for potential disciplinary action. 

The report marks one of the most explicit findings of systemic politicization within the Justice Department's hiring apparatus in over a decade, raising fresh questions about the long-term impact on the independence of the nation’s legal institution.
